data.title: OISC: The One-Instruction Set Computer
data.statement:
Do you want to take RISC architecture to the extreme? Have you always struggled to remember assembly? Then try building a <<One-Instruction Set Computer>> (OISC): a machine with a single instruction. There is not even an opcode, so there is no risk of forgetting it!

Your goal is to write an <<assembler>> for OISC Assembly and a <<virtual machine>> that runs the assembled program, including input and output.

<<Memory>>
- The memory has <<256 cells>> (addresses 0 to 255). Each cell holds an 8-bit value (0 to 255) and is initialized to 0.
- There are no registers. Execution starts at address 0.
- All arithmetic is done <<modulo 256>>. Negative numbers use two's complement: for example, -15 is stored as 11110001 in binary, i.e. 241.
- When a value is compared with zero, it is interpreted as a <<signed>> 8-bit number: 0 is zero, 1 to 127 are positive, 128 to 255 are negative (-128 to -1).

<<Syntax>>
- The source code is <<case-insensitive>> (SUBLEQ = subleq, @LOOP = @loop).
- Tokens are separated by spaces or tabs. Lines may have leading or trailing spaces or tabs, and blank lines may appear. Spaces are allowed around {{,}} and {{+}}.
- A negative number has no space between {{-}} and its digits.
- Each line contains any number of label definitions, optionally followed by one instruction or directive.
- The assembler fills the memory in source order, starting at address 0: each {{subleq}} takes the next 3 cells, each {{.data}} the next cell.

<<Labels>>
{{@}}[[name]]{{:}} gives [[name]] the address of the next memory cell filled.
- Names start with {{@}} followed by letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9) and underscores ({{_}}), with no space before the {{:}}.
- A label can be used before it is defined.
- A label can be followed by a non-negative offset: {{@}}[[name]]{{+}}[[k]] means the address of [[name]] plus [[k]], modulo 256.
- Two labels are predefined: {{@IN}} (address 254) and {{@OUT}} (address 255).

<<Instruction: subleq>>
{{subleq}} [[A]]{{,}} [[B]] [ {{,}} [[C]] ]
Each operand is an integer from 0 to 255 or a label (with an optional offset).
The instruction is assembled into <<3 consecutive cells>> holding A, B and C. If [[C]] is omitted, it is set to the address of the cell right after the instruction (the instruction's address + 3), so execution simply continues.
`Assembler    | Addr | Value
-------------+------+------------------
subleq 5,9   |  0   | 5
             |  1   | 9
             |  2   | 3   (C omitted: 2+1)
subleq 4,5,9 |  3   | 4
             |  4   | 5
             |  5   | 9   (explicit C)`

When executed, writing mem[ [[X]] ] for the value stored at address [[X]]:
1. compute r = (mem[ [[A]] ] - mem[ [[B]] ]) modulo 256 (mem[ [[A]] ] is read first, then mem[ [[B]] ]),
2. store r at address [[A]],
3. if r is <<less than or equal to zero>> (signed), jump to address [[C]]; otherwise continue at the next instruction (current address + 3).

<<Directive: .data>>
{{.data}} [[D]] stores [[D]] in the next memory cell. [[D]] is an integer from -128 to 255 or a label (with an optional offset).
`Assembler        | Addr | Value
-----------------+------+------
.data 10         |  0   | 10
.data -1         |  1   | 255
@x: .data @x+5   |  2   | 7`

<<Input and output>>
- Reading {{@IN}} (address 254) returns the next value of the input list. Writing to {{@IN}} has no effect.
- Writing to {{@OUT}} (address 255) outputs the value as an integer from 0 to 255. Reading {{@OUT}} always returns 0.

<<Halting>>
The program stops when:
- the next instruction to execute is at address {{@IN}} or {{@OUT}} (by a jump or by moving on to the next instruction), or
- an instruction reads {{@IN}} after all input values have been used. That instruction is cancelled: nothing is written and nothing is output.

Self-modifying code is allowed.

<<Full example>>
`Assembler            | Addr  | Output
---------------------+-------+-------
@lp:                 |       |
subleq @OUT,@lp+9    | 0-2   | 1
subleq @OUT,@dz+1    | 3-5   | 15
subleq @OUT,@pos     | 6-8   | 242
subleq @OUT,@OUT,@IN | 9-11  | 0
@dz:  .data 15       | 12    |
      .data -15      | 13    |
@pos: .data @dz+2    | 14    |`

- @lp is 0, @dz is 12 (four instructions of 3 cells each), @pos is 14.
- Line 1: @lp+9 is address 9, which holds the A operand of the 4th subleq, i.e. @OUT = 255 = -1. The result is 0-(-1) = 1: it is output and, being positive, execution continues.
- Line 2: @dz+1 is address 13, which holds -15 (241). Output: 0-(-15) = 15.
- Line 3: @pos holds @dz+2 = 14. Output: 0-14 = -14, i.e. 242.
- Line 4: 0-0 = 0 is output; since 0 ≤ 0, execution jumps to @IN and the program halts (and catches fire!).

The programs are always valid, the assembled code fits in addresses 0 to 253, and execution never reads an instruction beyond address 253.

<<References>>
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-instruction_set_computer
https://esolangs.org/wiki/Subleq
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two%27s_complement
